name: Drafting a Manuscript
title: Drafting a Manuscript
answer: Drafting a manuscript covers turning research results into a structured paper, including the title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, and references. It involves writing, revising, formatting, and preparing a document for submission to a journal or conference. AI assistance can help with summarising findings, checking the logical flow of sections, suggesting clearer phrasing, and keeping terminology consistent. The scope also includes managing citations and responding to reviewer comments during revision.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Drafting a manuscript covers turning research results into a structured paper, including the title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, and references. It involves writing, revising, formatting, and preparing a document for submission to a journal or conference. AI assistance can help with summarising findings, checking the logical flow of sections, suggesting clearer phrasing, and keeping terminology consistent. The scope also includes managing citations and responding to reviewer comments during revision.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Drafting tools typically run on standard office software, cloud document editors, and reference managers. AI features may be embedded in these editors or accessed through separate language model interfaces. The underlying models are usually large language models trained on broad text corpora, sometimes fine-tuned on academic writing. Local or institutional servers may be used where privacy or data handling rules require it.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A researcher usually starts from an outline or a set of results, then writes sections in sequence or iteratively. AI can generate draft paragraphs from notes, rephrase sentences for clarity, suggest alternative structures, and check for missing elements such as a clear research question or a limitations section. The human author reviews every generated sentence, verifies facts and citations, and decides what to keep. Peer review feedback then leads to further revision, often with AI used to track changes or summarise reviewer comments.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Authors remain responsible for the accuracy and originality of the manuscript. Many journals require disclosure of AI use in drafting, and some prohibit AI-generated text in certain sections. Risks include fabricated citations, paraphrased text that is too close to a source, and loss of the author's own voice. Provenance matters: any claim or reference must be traceable to the original paper, not to a search tool or model output. Institutional policies and publisher guidelines set the rules for what is acceptable.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Drafting support is moving toward more integrated workflows, where AI can pull from a researcher's own notes, data files, and reference library while drafting. Future tools may better preserve citation provenance and flag unsupported claims in real time. There is also work on making AI suggestions more transparent, so authors can see why a sentence was changed. The likely direction is not fully automated writing but closer assistance with structure, consistency, and compliance with journal requirements.
